metadata.description: Three plywood laminations for one shelf gusset, cut flat and glued face to face

prompt:
The shelf gussets are laminated: each one is three flat pieces of 6 mm ply, glued face to face after cutting. I need the set modelled as one part called `gusset` and the nested cut file for it.

The stock thickness, the blank size and the three flat sizes are all in `globals.py` - read them through `hc`. All three pieces lie flat in the sheet, every one of them spanning z = 0 to one sheet thickness, and they are three separate solids in the part (they are three separate pieces of ply). Label them `web`, `spacer` and `cleat`. In millimetres:

- `web` is a right triangle: the two legs are 100 along X and 60 along Y, meeting at the right angle;
- `spacer` is a 60 x 40 rectangle;
- `cleat` is a 90 x 25 rectangle.

Lay them out in the part so none of them overlap - the layout inside the part does not have to be tight, the cut file is nested for you.

The shop cuts one set per 210 x 125 mm blank, so declare that blank as the part's stock blank size in its manufacturing metadata, along with a description, the material (`6 mm Baltic birch plywood`), the process (`laser_cut`) and the stock form. Then export the nested cut file as DXF so all three profiles come out nested on that single blank.

Build the part before you export it.

Tool-call budget: 20 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.

prompt:
Design an L-bracket in this project as the part `bracket`.

The bracket is a 60 mm (X) by 40 mm (Y) base plate, 6 mm thick, lying on the XY plane with its footprint centred on the origin and its underside at z = 0. Along the base plate's -Y edge stands a 6 mm thick wall of the same 60 mm length; the wall rises so the bracket's overall height is 40 mm. Blend the inner corner where the wall meets the top of the base plate with a 4 mm radius fillet.

Drill two 6 mm diameter through-holes in the base plate. Their centres are 12 mm in from each end of the plate (12 mm from the -X end and 12 mm from the +X end) and 14 mm in from the plate's +Y edge.

The project's `globals.py` already carries the plate thickness and the bracket envelope: read them through `hc` instead of repeating the numbers. The project also contains an inspection gauge part (`hole_gauge`) whose go-pins the acceptance checks fit through your holes - leave it exactly as it is.

Name the part `bracket`, build it, and export it as STEP when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 20 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

prompt:
I want a cat step for the hallway wall - one of a run of climbing shelves, so this one has to be right before I cut the rest.

It is two pieces of the 18 mm ply we have in stock. The tread is a rectangle 300 mm wide (along X) and 200 mm deep (out from the wall), lying flat with its back edge against the wall and its underside level with the top of the bracket. Put the underside on z = 0 and keep the tread centred left-to-right on x = 0, so it spans z = 0 up to one panel thickness. The two front corners - the outer corners furthest from the wall - want rounding off with a 25 mm radius so the cat cannot catch a sharp corner coming down.

Under it goes a single triangular gusset, the same 18 mm ply, standing on edge and centred on x = 0. It is a right triangle: the vertical leg against the wall, the horizontal leg flat against the tread's underside reaching 140 mm out from the wall, and the hypotenuse running from that far point back down to the wall 160 mm below the tread. The gusset must touch the tread's underside along its whole top edge and must sit flat against the wall - it cannot float in front of the wall or cut into it.

The project already contains a `wall_plane` part: that is the wall itself, reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Call the tread part `shelf` and the bracket part `gusset`. The panel thickness and the wall's position are in `globals.py`; read them through `hc`. Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 52 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

The laser shop rejected the cut file for the `vent_panel` part in this project. The part builds fine - two of its features simply cannot be cut on their machine, and they want it fixed before they will quote it.

Run the manufacturability check for the process the part declares and read what it reports. Then repair the geometry.

This is a repair-only task: the design intent does not change. Keep the 80 x 50 mm blank, one sheet thick, and keep the service notch exactly where it is (16 mm along X, 10 mm deep, cut in from the +Y edge). What is wrong is that two feature sizes were typed into the script as placeholders instead of being read from the project: the vent bore diameter and the radius on the notch's two inner corners are both declared in `globals.py`, like every other dimension the script uses. Read them through `hc`.

When you are done, the laser_cut rule pack must report no findings at all for the minimum-cut-feature rule and the internal-radius rule. Build the part to prove the repair.

Tool-call budget: 12 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
I want a cat step for the hallway wall - one of a run of climbing shelves, so this one has to be right before I cut the rest.

It is two pieces of the 18 mm ply we have in stock. The tread is a rectangle 300 mm wide (along X) and 200 mm deep (out from the wall), lying flat with its back edge against the wall and its underside level with the top of the bracket. Put the underside on z = 0 and keep the tread centred left-to-right on x = 0, so it spans z = 0 up to one panel thickness. The two front corners - the outer corners furthest from the wall - want rounding off with a 25 mm radius so the cat cannot catch a sharp corner coming down.

Under it goes a single triangular gusset, the same 18 mm ply, standing on edge and centred on x = 0. It is a right triangle: the vertical leg against the wall, the horizontal leg flat against the tread's underside reaching 140 mm out from the wall, and the hypotenuse running from that far point back down to the wall 160 mm below the tread. The gusset must touch the tread's underside along its whole top edge and must sit flat against the wall - it cannot float in front of the wall or cut into it.

The project already contains a `wall_plane` part: that is the wall itself, reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Call the tread part `shelf` and the bracket part `gusset`. The panel thickness and the wall's position are in `globals.py`; read them through `hc`. Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 52 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.

prompt:
I want a cat step for the hallway wall - one of a run of climbing shelves, so this one has to be right before I cut the rest.

It is two pieces of the 18 mm ply we have in stock. The tread is a rectangle 300 mm wide (along X) and 200 mm deep (out from the wall), lying flat with its back edge against the wall and its underside level with the top of the bracket. Put the underside on z = 0 and keep the tread centred left-to-right on x = 0, so it spans z = 0 up to one panel thickness. The two front corners - the outer corners furthest from the wall - want rounding off with a 25 mm radius so the cat cannot catch a sharp corner coming down.

Under it goes a single triangular gusset, the same 18 mm ply, standing on edge and centred on x = 0. It is a right triangle: the vertical leg against the wall, the horizontal leg flat against the tread's underside reaching 140 mm out from the wall, and the hypotenuse running from that far point back down to the wall 160 mm below the tread. The gusset must touch the tread's underside along its whole top edge and must sit flat against the wall - it cannot float in front of the wall or cut into it.

The project already contains a `wall_plane` part: that is the wall itself, reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Call the tread part `shelf` and the bracket part `gusset`. The panel thickness and the wall's position are in `globals.py`; read them through `hc`. Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 52 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.

What is wrong is that two feature sizes were typed into the script as placeholders instead of being read from the project: the vent bore diameter and the radius on the notch's two inner corners are both declared in `globals.py`, like every other dimension the script uses. Read them through `hc`.

Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.

prompt:
Design a tabbed open tray to be cut from 6 mm sheet on the CNC router. It needs three parts: `base`, `walls` and `flat_layout`.

The stock thickness, the kerf clearance and the tray's interface dimensions are already in the project's `globals.py` - read them through `hc` rather than repeating the numbers.

Geometry, all in millimetres:

- `base` is the base panel: a 110 x 90 blank, one sheet thick, centred on the origin and lying under the tray with its top face on z = 0 (so it spans z = -6 to 0). It carries eight through slots, two for each wall (below).
- `walls` is the four assembled walls. They stand on the base's top face and rise 40 mm (z = 0 to 40). Each wall is one sheet thick. The two long walls run the full 100 mm along X with their outer faces at y = -40 and y = +40. The two short walls run along Y between the long walls' inner faces (68 mm long) with their outer faces at x = -50 and x = +50.
- Every wall carries two tabs on its bottom edge: one sheet thick, 12 mm long, hanging one sheet thickness below the wall (z = -6 to 0), centred a quarter of that wall's length in from each end - so the long walls' tabs sit at x = -25 and x = +25, and the short walls' tabs at y = -17 and y = +17.
- The base's eight slots are the tab footprints grown by the kerf on every side: each slot is (tab length + kerf) by (sheet thickness + kerf), cut all the way through, centred on its tab. The tabs must pass through without touching the slot walls, while the walls' bottom edges rest on the base.
- `flat_layout` is the cut file: the same five panels laid out flat on the sheet, all of them spanning z = 0 to 6 and none of them overlapping. This is the part the shop cuts, so its as-built DXF must show exactly five outer profiles (the base panel's slots are interior cut-outs of its profile).

Build all three parts and export `flat_layout` as DXF when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 32 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

prompt:
Design a tabbed open tray to be cut from 6 mm sheet on the CNC router. It needs three parts: `base`, `walls` and `flat_layout`.

The stock thickness, the kerf clearance and the tray's interface dimensions are already in the project's `globals.py` - read them through `hc` rather than repeating the numbers.

Geometry, all in millimetres:

- `base` is the base panel: a 110 x 90 blank, one sheet thick, centred on the origin and lying under the tray with its top face on z = 0 (so it spans z = -6 to 0). It carries eight through slots, two for each wall (below).
- `walls` is the four assembled walls. They stand on the base's top face and rise 40 mm (z = 0 to 40). Each wall is one sheet thick. The two long walls run the full 100 mm along X with their outer faces at y = -40 and y = +40. The two short walls run along Y between the long walls' inner faces (68 mm long) with their outer faces at x = -50 and x = +50.
- Every wall carries two tabs on its bottom edge: one sheet thick, 12 mm long, hanging one sheet thickness below the wall (z = -6 to 0), centred a quarter of that wall's length in from each end - so the long walls' tabs sit at x = -25 and x = +25, and the short walls' tabs at y = -17 and y = +17.
- The base's eight slots are the tab footprints grown by the kerf on every side: each slot is (tab length + kerf) by (sheet thickness + kerf), cut all the way through, centred on its tab. The tabs must pass through without touching the slot walls, while the walls' bottom edges rest on the base.
- `flat_layout` is the cut file: the same five panels laid out flat on the sheet, all of them spanning z = 0 to 6 and none of them overlapping. This is the part the shop cuts, so its as-built DXF must show exactly five outer profiles (the base panel's slots are interior cut-outs of its profile).

Build all three parts and export `flat_layout` as DXF when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 32 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

prompt:
Design a tabbed open tray to be cut from 6 mm sheet on the CNC router. It needs three parts: `base`, `walls` and `flat_layout`.

The stock thickness, the kerf clearance and the tray's interface dimensions are already in the project's `globals.py` - read them through `hc` rather than repeating the numbers.

Geometry, all in millimetres:

- `base` is the base panel: a 110 x 90 blank, one sheet thick, centred on the origin and lying under the tray with its top face on z = 0 (so it spans z = -6 to 0). It carries eight through slots, two for each wall (below).
- `walls` is the four assembled walls. They stand on the base's top face and rise 40 mm (z = 0 to 40). Each wall is one sheet thick. The two long walls run the full 100 mm along X with their outer faces at y = -40 and y = +40. The two short walls run along Y between the long walls' inner faces (68 mm long) with their outer faces at x = -50 and x = +50.
- Every wall carries two tabs on its bottom edge: one sheet thick, 12 mm long, hanging one sheet thickness below the wall (z = -6 to 0), centred a quarter of that wall's length in from each end - so the long walls' tabs sit at x = -25 and x = +25, and the short walls' tabs at y = -17 and y = +17.
- The base's eight slots are the tab footprints grown by the kerf on every side: each slot is (tab length + kerf) by (sheet thickness + kerf), cut all the way through, centred on its tab. The tabs must pass through without touching the slot walls, while the walls' bottom edges rest on the base.
- `flat_layout` is the cut file: the same five panels laid out flat on the sheet, all of them spanning z = 0 to 6 and none of them overlapping. This is the part the shop cuts, so its as-built DXF must show exactly five outer profiles (the base panel's slots are interior cut-outs of its profile).

Build all three parts and export `flat_layout` as DXF when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 32 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
The `bracket` part in this project is the finished L-bracket: 60 x 40 base plate, 6 mm thick, upstanding wall, two 6 mm through-holes 12 mm in from each end and 14 mm in from the +Y edge. It now has to mount with M5 socket-head cap screws, and the mating part sits flat on the plate's top face, so no screw head may stand proud of it.

Re-detail the two mounting holes for M5 socket-head cap screws: a 5.5 mm clearance hole through the plate, and a 10 mm diameter counterbore 5 mm deep cut down from the plate's top face. Keep the hole centres, the envelope, the wall and the corner fillet exactly as they are.

Then add a second part called `screws` holding the hardware itself: two M5 socket-head cap screws from the parts store (`screw_socket_head_m5`) with a 16 mm shank, one seated in each counterbore. The store's envelope is a 8.5 mm diameter head 5 mm high, a 5 mm diameter shank hanging below it, and a 4 mm across-flats hex socket 3 mm deep in the head; its origin sits on the head bearing face with the head above and the shank below, so a screw seated on the counterbore floor has its head exactly flush with the plate's top face.

The project also contains a `head_gauge` part - reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.

Design an L-bracket in this project as the part `bracket`.

The bracket is a 60 mm (X) by 40 mm (Y) base plate, 6 mm thick, lying on the XY plane with its footprint centred on the origin and its underside at z = 0. Along the base plate's -Y edge stands a 6 mm thick wall of the same 60 mm length; the wall rises so the bracket's overall height is 40 mm. Blend the inner corner where the wall meets the top of the base plate with a 4 mm radius fillet.

Drill two 6 mm diameter through-holes in the base plate. Their centres are 12 mm in from each end of the plate (12 mm from the -X end and 12 mm from the +X end) and 14 mm in from the plate's +Y edge.

The project's `globals.py` already carries the plate thickness and the bracket envelope: read them through `hc` instead of repeating the numbers. The project also contains an inspection gauge part (`hole_gauge`) whose go-pins the acceptance checks fit through your holes - leave it exactly as it is.

Tool-call budget: 20 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.

prompt:
I want a cat step for the hallway wall - one of a run of climbing shelves, so this one has to be right before I cut the rest.

It is two pieces of the 18 mm ply we have in stock. The tread is a rectangle 300 mm wide (along X) and 200 mm deep (out from the wall), lying flat with its back edge against the wall and its underside level with the top of the bracket. Put the underside on z = 0 and keep the tread centred left-to-right on x = 0, so it spans z = 0 up to one panel thickness. prompt:
I want a cat step for the hallway wall - one of a run of climbing shelves, so this one has to be right before I cut the rest.

It is two pieces of the 18 mm ply we have in stock. The tread is a rectangle 300 mm wide (along X) and 200 mm deep (out from the wall), lying flat with its back edge against the wall and its underside level with the top of the bracket. Put the underside on z = 0 and keep the tread centred left-to-right on x = 0, so it spans z = 0 up to one panel thickness. The two front corners - the outer corners furthest from the wall - want rounding off with a 25 mm radius so the cat cannot catch a sharp corner coming down.

Under it goes a single triangular gusset, the same 18 mm ply, standing on edge and centred on x = 0. It is a right triangle: the vertical leg against the wall, the horizontal leg flat against the tread's underside reaching 140 mm out from the wall, and the hypotenuse running from that far point back down to the wall 160 mm below the tread. The gusset must touch the tread's underside along its whole top edge and must sit flat against the wall - it cannot float in front of the wall or cut into it.

The project already contains a `wall_plane` part: that is the wall itself, reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Call the tread part `shelf` and the bracket part `gusset`. The panel thickness and the wall's position are in `globals.py`; read them through `hc`. Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 52 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

prompt:
The laser shop rejected the cut file for the `vent_panel` part in this project. The part builds fine - two of its features simply cannot be cut on their machine, and they want it fixed before they will quote it.

Run the manufacturability check for the process the part declares and read what it reports. Then repair the geometry.

This is a repair-only task: the design intent does not change. Keep the 80 x 50 mm blank, one sheet thick, and keep the service notch exactly where it is (16 mm along X, 10 mm deep, cut in from the +Y edge). What is wrong is that two feature sizes were typed into the script as placeholders instead of being read from the project: the vent bore diameter and the radius on the notch's two inner corners are both declared in `globals.py`, like every other dimension the script uses. Read them through `hc`.

When you are done, the laser_cut rule pack must report no findings at all for the minimum-cut-feature rule and the internal-radius rule. Build the part to prove the repair.

Tool-call budget: 12 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.

metadata.description: Fan-shroud vent panel: notched blank with a single vent bore

prompt:
The laser shop rejected the cut file for the `vent_panel` part in this project. The part builds fine - two of its features simply cannot be cut on their machine, and they want it fixed before they will quote it.

Run the manufacturability check for the process the part declares and read what it reports. Then repair the geometry.

This is a repair-only task: the design intent does not change. Keep the 80 x 50 mm blank, one sheet thick, and keep the service notch exactly where it is (16 mm along X, 10 mm deep, cut in from the +Y edge). What is wrong is that two feature sizes were typed into the script as placeholders instead of being read from the project: the vent bore diameter and the radius on the notch's two inner corners are both declared in `globals.py`, like every other dimension the script uses. Read them through `hc`.

When you are done, the laser_cut rule pack must report no findings at all for the minimum-cut-feature rule and the internal-radius rule. Build the part to prove the repair.

Tool-call budget: 12 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.

metadata.description: Three-piece laminated shelf gusset cut set

prompt:
The shelf gussets are laminated: each one is three flat pieces of 6 mm ply, glued face to face after cutting. I need the set modelled as one part called `gusset` and the nested cut file for it.

The stock thickness, the blank size and the three flat sizes are all in `globals.py` - read them through `hc`. All three pieces lie flat in the sheet, every one of them spanning z = 0 to one sheet thickness, and they are three separate solids in the part (they are three separate pieces of ply). Label them `web`, `spacer` and `cleat`. In millimetres:

- `web` is a right triangle: the two legs are 100 along X and 60 along Y, meeting at the right angle;
- `spacer` is a 60 x 40 rectangle;
- `cleat` is a 90 x 25 rectangle.

Lay them out in the part so none of them overlap - the layout inside the part does not have to be tight, the cut file is nested for you.

The shop cuts one set per 210 x 125 mm blank, so declare that blank as the part's stock blank size in its manufacturing metadata, along with a description, the material (`6 mm Baltic birch plywood`), the process (`laser_cut`) and the stock form. Then export the nested cut file as DXF so all three profiles come out nested on that single blank.

Build the part before you export it.

Tool-call budget: 20 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

metadata.description: Three-piece laminated shelf gusset cut set

prompt:
The shelf gussets are laminated: each one is three flat pieces of 6 mm ply, glued face to face after cutting. I need the set modelled as one part called `gusset` and the nested cut file for it.

The stock thickness, the blank size and the three flat sizes are all in `globals.py` - read them through `hc`. All three pieces lie flat in the sheet, every one of them spanning z = 0 to one sheet thickness, and they are three separate solids in the part (they are three separate pieces of ply). Label them `web`, `spacer` and `cleat`. In millimetres:

- `web` is a right triangle: the two legs are 100 along X and 60 along Y, meeting at the right angle;
- `spacer` is a 60 x 40 rectangle;
- `cleat` is a 90 x 25 rectangle.

Lay them out in the part so none of them overlap - the layout inside the part does not have to be tight, the cut file is nested for you.

The shop cuts one set per 210 x 125 mm blank, so declare that blank as the part's stock blank size in its manufacturing metadata, along with a description, the material (`6 mm Baltic birch plywood`), the process (`laser_cut`) and the stock form. Then export the nested cut file as DXF so all three profiles come out nested on that single blank.

Build the part before you export it.

Tool-call budget: 20 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
Design a tabbed open tray to be cut from 6 mm sheet on the CNC router. It needs three parts: `base`, `walls` and `flat_layout`.

The stock thickness, the kerf clearance and the tray's interface dimensions are already in the project's `globals.py` - read them through `hc` rather than repeating the numbers.

Geometry, all in millimetres:

- `base` is the base panel: a 110 x 90 blank, one sheet thick, centred on the origin and lying under the tray with its top face on z = 0 (so it spans z = -6 to 0). It carries eight through slots, two for each wall (below).
- `walls` is the four assembled walls. They stand on the base's top face and rise 40 mm (z = 0 to 40). Each wall is one sheet thick. The two long walls run the full 100 mm along X with their outer faces at y = -40 and y = +40. The two short walls run along Y between the long walls' inner faces (68 mm long) with their outer faces at x = -50 and x = +50.
- Every wall carries two tabs on its bottom edge: one sheet thick, 12 mm long, hanging one sheet thickness below the wall (z = -6 to 0), centred a quarter of that wall's length in from each end - so the long walls' tabs sit at x = -25 and x = +25, and the short walls' tabs at y = -17 and y = +17.
- The base's eight slots are the tab footprints grown by the kerf on every side: each slot is (tab length + kerf) by (sheet thickness + kerf), cut all the way through, centred on its tab. The tabs must pass through without touching the slot walls, while the walls' bottom edges rest on the base.
- `flat_layout` is the cut file: the same five panels laid out flat on the sheet, all of them spanning z = 0 to 6 and none of them overlapping. This is the part the shop cuts, so its as-built DXF must show exactly five outer profiles (the base panel's slots are interior cut-outs of its profile).

Build all three parts and export `flat_layout` as DXF when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 32 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Work in millimetres. When you are done, summarise what you built and the checks you relied on.

prompt:
Design a tabbed open tray to be cut from 6 mm sheet on the CNC router. It needs three parts: `base`, `walls` and `flat_layout`.

The stock thickness, the kerf clearance and the tray's interface dimensions are already in the project's `globals.py` - read them through `hc` rather than repeating the numbers.

Geometry, all in millimetres:

- `base` is the base panel: a 110 x 90 blank, one sheet thick, centred on the origin and lying under the tray with its top face on z = 0 (so it spans z = -6 to 0). It carries eight through slots, two for each wall (below).
- `walls` is the four assembled walls. They stand on the base's top face and rise 40 mm (z = 0 to 40). Each wall is one sheet thick. The two long walls run the full 100 mm along X with their outer faces at y = -40 and y = +40. The two short walls run along Y between the long walls' inner faces (68 mm long) with their outer faces at x = -50 and x = +50.
- Every wall carries two tabs on its bottom edge: one sheet thick, 12 mm long, hanging one sheet thickness below the wall (z = -6 to 0), centred a quarter of that wall's length in from each end - so the long walls' tabs sit at x = -25 and x = +25, and the short walls' tabs at y = -17 and y = +17.
- The base's eight slots are the tab footprints grown by the kerf on every side: each slot is (tab length + kerf) by (sheet thickness + kerf), cut all the way through, centred on its tab. The tabs must pass through without touching the slot walls, while the walls' bottom edges rest on the base.
- `flat_layout` is the cut file: the same five panels laid out flat on the sheet, all of them spanning z = 0 to 6 and none of them overlapping. This is the part the shop cuts, so its as-built DXF must show exactly five outer profiles (the base panel's slots are interior cut-outs of its profile).

Build all three parts and export `flat_layout` as DXF when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 32 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.

prompt:
The `bracket` part in this project is the finished L-bracket: 60 x 40 base plate, 6 mm thick, upstanding wall, two 6 mm through-holes 12 mm in from each end and 14 mm in from the +Y edge. It now has to mount with M5 socket-head cap screws, and the mating part sits flat on the plate's top face, so no screw head may stand proud of it.

Re-detail the two mounting holes for M5 socket-head cap screws: a 5.5 mm clearance hole through the plate, and a 10 mm diameter counterbore 5 mm deep cut down from the plate's top face. Keep the hole centres, the envelope, the wall and the corner fillet exactly as they are.

Then add a second part called `screws` holding the hardware itself: two M5 socket-head cap screws from the parts store (`screw_socket_head_m5`) with a 16 mm shank, one seated in each counterbore. The store's envelope is a 8.5 mm diameter head 5 mm high, a 5 mm diameter shank hanging below it, and a 4 mm across-flats hex socket 3 mm deep in the head; its origin sits on the head bearing face with the head above and the shank below, so a screw seated on the counterbore floor has its head exactly flush with the plate's top face.

The project also contains a `head_gauge` part - reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 27 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.

prompt:
The `bracket` part in this project is the finished L-bracket: 60 x 40 base plate, 6 mm thick, upstanding wall, two 6 mm through-holes 12 mm in from each end and 14 mm in from the +Y edge. It now has to mount with M5 socket-head cap screws, and the mating part sits flat on the plate's top face, so no screw head may stand proud of it.

Re-detail the two mounting holes for M5 socket-head cap screws: a 5.5 mm clearance hole through the plate, and a 10 mm diameter counterbore 5 mm deep cut down from the plate's top face. Keep the hole centres, the envelope, the wall and the corner fillet exactly as they are.

Then add a second part called `screws` holding the hardware itself: two M5 socket-head cap screws from the parts store (`screw_socket_head_m5`) with a 16 mm shank, one seated in each counterbore. The store's envelope is a 8.5 mm diameter head 5 mm high, a 5 mm diameter shank hanging below it, and a 4 mm across-flats hex socket 3 mm deep in the head; its origin sits on the head bearing face with the head above and the shank below, so a screw seated on the counterbore floor has its head exactly flush with the plate's top face.

The project also contains a `head_gauge` part - reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 27 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.

prompt:
The `bracket` part in this project is the finished L-bracket: 60 x 40 base plate, 6 mm thick, upstanding wall, two 6 mm through-holes 12 mm in from each end and 14 mm in from the +Y edge. It now has to mount with M5 socket-head cap screws, and the mating part sits flat on the plate's top face, so no screw head may stand proud of it.

Re-detail the two mounting holes for M5 socket-head cap screws: a 5.5 mm clearance hole through the plate, and a 10 mm diameter counterbore 5 mm deep cut down from the plate's top face. Keep the hole centres, the envelope, the wall and the corner fillet exactly as they are.

Then add a second part called `screws` holding the hardware itself: two M5 socket-head cap screws from the parts store (`screw_socket_head_m5`) with a 16 mm shank, one seated in each counterbore. The store's envelope is a 8.5 mm diameter head 5 mm high, a 5 mm diameter shank hanging below it, and a 4 mm across-flats hex socket 3 mm deep in the head; its origin sits on the head bearing face with the head above and the shank below, so a screw seated on the counterbore floor has its head exactly flush with the plate's top face.

The project also contains a `head_gauge` part - reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 27 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

All dimensions are millimetres. Build the geometry before you report, and say which measurements you verified.
